title: Cyberspace, network security and data transfer

pages.c07-p03: Define the term malware and describe the following forms of malware: virus, Trojan horse, worm, key logger and spyware

q.q: Which is the best definition of cybercrime?
o: Any software designed to damage or disrupt a computer system
Any attack that physically damages computer hardware
Any use of a work computer that breaks company policy
Any crime committed using a computer, a network or the internet
q.why: Cybercrime covers any crime where a computer, network or the internet is used. Software designed to damage or disrupt is the definition of malware, not cybercrime.

q.q: What does the term cybersecurity mean?
o: Any crime that is committed using a computer, network or the internet
The UK law that makes unauthorised access to computers an offence
Software that scans files for the signatures of known malware
The methods used to protect computers, networks and data from attacks
q.why: Cybersecurity is the protection of computers, networks and data. Crimes committed with a computer are cybercrime; the law is the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

q.q: Which UK law makes unauthorised access to computer material a criminal offence?
o: Data Protection Act 2018
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access and deliberately impairing a computer system offences.

q.q: Which is the best description of hacking?
o: Software that copies itself and spreads across a network
Flooding a server with requests so genuine users cannot connect
Sending bulk unwanted messages to a large number of people
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or its data
q.why: Hacking is a person gaining unauthorised access. A worm spreads itself, DoS floods a server and spamming is bulk messaging.

q.q: A criminal sends millions of fake requests to a council's website so residents cannot pay their rates online. Which threat is this?
o: Denial of service
Hacking
Spamming
Data theft
q.why: Flooding a server with requests so genuine users cannot use it is a denial of service attack. Nothing is accessed or stolen, so it is not hacking or data theft.

q.q: A denial of service attack is launched from thousands of computers at the same time. What is this called?
o: A worm attack spreading across the network
A mass phishing attack on the server
A cyber stalking attack on the website
A distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack
q.why: When the flood of requests comes from thousands of computers at once it is a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack.

q.q: Criminals use a victim's stolen name, address and bank details to apply for credit in the victim's name. This is mainly the result of which threat?
o: Denial of service
Spamming
Data theft
Cyber stalking
q.why: Data theft often leads to identity fraud, where criminals use stolen details to pretend to be the victim.

q.q: Which is the best description of cyber stalking?
o: Posting untrue statements online that harm a person's reputation
Secretly recording every key that a person presses on a keyboard
Using technology to repeatedly harass, track or frighten a person
Tricking a person into handing over their passwords or bank details
q.why: Cyber stalking is repeated harassment, tracking or frightening of a person using technology. Untrue statements are cyber defamation; recording keys is a key logger.

q.q: Why is an employee visiting pornographic sites on a work PC a cybersecurity risk to the organisation?
o: Adult sites are a common place for malware to be hidden, which can infect the network
Visiting the sites counts as a denial of service attack on the company's web server
The sites automatically encrypt the company's files so that they can no longer be read
The sites copy the employee's password into the company's firewall rules
q.why: Adult sites are a common hiding place for malware, so downloading from them at work can infect the office network (as well as breaking acceptable use policies).

q.q: Which statement about hacking and malware is correct?
o: Hacking and malware are two different names for exactly the same threat
Malware is a person gaining unauthorised access; hacking is the software
Hacking can only take place after malware has been installed on a computer
Hacking is a person gaining unauthorised access; malware is software
q.why: Hacking is done by a person; malware is software. A hacker may use malware, but the terms are not interchangeable.

q.q: Which description of a denial of service attack would earn full marks, because it gives what it is and its effect?
o: It is a type of attack on a website that is carried out by a hacker somewhere on the internet
It floods a web server with requests so genuine customers cannot reach it, losing the business sales
It floods a web server with a very large number of requests sent from many fake accounts at once
It is a type of malware hidden in an email attachment that spreads to every contact in the address book
q.why: For 'describe a threat' you need what it is plus its effect. Only the first answer gives both; one just says 'an attack', one has no effect and one describes a worm.

q.q: In which example is the computer the TOOL used to commit the crime, rather than the target?
o: Sending threatening messages to follow and frighten someone
Breaking into a council's server to change its records
Crashing a ticket website with a flood of fake requests
Planting malware that deletes files on a company's network
q.why: In cyber stalking the computer is used as a tool to harm a person. In the other examples the computer system itself is the target.

q.q: Which is the best description of digital forgery?
o: Deliberately and falsely altering digital content to deceive
Posting untrue statements online that harm someone's reputation
Sending messages that pretend to be from a trusted organisation
Sending bulk unwanted adverts and scams to many people at once
q.why: Digital forgery is falsely altering digital content such as photos or documents. Untrue statements are cyber defamation; fake trusted messages are phishing.

q.q: Someone edits a scanned driving licence to change the photo and the date of birth. Which threat is this?
o: Cyber defamation
Phishing
Digital forgery
Data theft
q.why: Falsely altering a digital document to deceive is digital forgery.

q.q: A rival business posts on a forum that a Newry hair salon uses dirty equipment. The claim is untrue and the salon loses customers. Which threat is this?
o: Cyber defamation
Digital forgery
Spamming
Cyber stalking
q.why: Posting untrue statements online that harm the reputation of a person or organisation is cyber defamation.

q.q: Which is the best description of spamming?
o: Sending one fake message to a person to steal their password or card details
Sending bulk unwanted messages, usually adverts or scams, to many people
Flooding a web server with requests so that genuine users cannot connect
Repeatedly sending threatening messages to one person to frighten them
q.why: Spamming is bulk unwanted messaging. A targeted trick to steal details is phishing, flooding a server is DoS and repeated threats to one person is cyber stalking.

q.q: Which is an effect of spamming?
o: It wastes time, fills storage and uses bandwidth
It deletes files as soon as the message is opened
It records each key the user presses on the keyboard
It stops genuine customers reaching a web server
q.why: Spam wastes time, fills storage and uses bandwidth, and often carries phishing links or malware.

q.q: Which description of phishing includes all three ideas needed for full marks?
o: A message pretending to be from a trusted source that tricks users into giving personal details
A message sent to thousands of people at once advertising products they did not ask for
A message pretending to be from a bank that is sent out to thousands of its customers
A message that tricks users into opening an attachment so that a virus is installed
q.why: Phishing needs: pretends to be from a trusted source, tricks the user, and aims to obtain personal details. The others each miss at least one idea.

q.q: A text claims to be from a delivery company about a missed parcel and gives a link asking for card details to rebook. Which threat is this?
o: Spamming
Phishing
Digital forgery
Hacking
q.why: It pretends to come from a trusted organisation to trick the person into giving card details, so it is phishing, not just spam.

q.q: Which statement about spam and phishing is correct?
o: All spam is phishing, because spam always asks for details
Phishing is any bulk unwanted message sent to many people
Spam and phishing are two names for the same threat
Some spam is phishing, but not all spam is phishing
q.why: Spam is any bulk unwanted message; phishing is a deliberate trick to steal personal details. Some spam is phishing, but not all.

q.q: What do digital forgery, cyber defamation, spamming and phishing have in common?
o: They all need malware installed on the victim's computer
They all work by flooding a server with traffic
They involve deceiving or misleading people
They all need a hacker to break into a network first
q.why: These four threats all involve deceiving or misleading people, either by faking content or by pretending to be someone trustworthy.

q.q: Which effect is most closely linked to digital forgery?
o: A business losing customers because of untrue posts made about it online
An inbox filled with junk messages that waste time and use up storage
A website that genuine customers cannot reach while it is under attack
Fake identity documents or certificates that help other crimes such as fraud
q.why: Digital forgery creates fake documents, certificates or evidence that help other crimes. Lost customers from untrue posts is the effect of cyber defamation.

q.q: Which effect is most closely linked to cyber defamation?
o: Fake certificates are used to apply for a job the person is not qualified for
Stolen passwords are used to empty the victim's bank account
A business loses customers and the owner may take legal action
A school network slows down because messages are filling its storage
q.why: Cyber defamation harms a reputation, which can cost a business customers and cause distress; victims may take legal action.

q.q: What is the usual result of a successful phishing attack?
o: The victim's web server is flooded so that genuine customers cannot reach it
The victim's photos are altered and shared to embarrass them in public
The victim's computer slows down because its storage fills with junk adverts
Stolen passwords and bank details are used for identity fraud or to empty accounts
q.why: Phishing aims to obtain personal details such as passwords and bank details, which are then used for identity fraud or to empty accounts.

q.q: Which definition of malware would examiners give full credit?
o: Software designed to damage or disrupt a system, or to gain unauthorised access to it
Malicious software that has been found on a computer system by a scan
Any software that contains bugs and causes the computer to crash
Any software that has been installed without buying a licence for it
q.why: 'Malicious software' alone is not enough; the definition must say what it is designed to do: damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access.

q.q: Which type of malware needs a host file and spreads when that file is run?
o: Worm
Trojan horse
Key logger
Virus
q.why: A virus attaches itself to a host file or program and runs when that file is opened. A worm needs no host.

q.q: Which malware copies itself and spreads across a network on its own, for example by emailing itself to every contact?
o: Virus
Trojan horse
Spyware
Worm
q.why: A worm needs no host file and spreads by itself across a network.

q.q: Which statement about a Trojan horse is correct?
o: It attaches itself to a host file and copies itself into others
It does not copy itself; it tricks the user into installing it
It copies itself and spreads across a network on its own
It is a virus that has been disguised as a free game
q.why: A Trojan is disguised as useful software and relies on the user installing it. It does not replicate, so calling it a virus can lose the mark.

q.q: Staff notice that the school network has slowed right down, although no files appear to be damaged. Which malware is the most likely cause?
o: A worm
A virus
A key logger
A Trojan horse
q.why: The typical sign of a worm is the network slowing down as it uses up bandwidth spreading itself. A virus is more often noticed by corrupted or missing files.

q.q: A customer types her email address and password into a banking site. Later a criminal logs into her account. Which malware most likely recorded the password as she typed it?
o: A key logger
A worm
A virus
A Trojan horse
q.why: A key logger secretly records every key pressed and sends the log to the criminal.

q.q: After installing a free screensaver, a user's PC runs slowly and details of every website she visits are being sent to an advertising company. Which malware is this?
o: A worm
Spyware
A key logger
A virus
q.why: Spyware is often bundled with free downloads, monitors activity such as websites visited and sends it to a third party; it also uses memory and slows the PC.

q.q: Which malware may stay hidden in a file until a trigger, such as a particular date, and then delete or corrupt data?
o: Worm
Spyware
Virus
Key logger
q.why: A virus attaches to a file and may wait for a trigger such as a date before deleting or corrupting data.

q.q: Which malware is most associated with opening a 'back door' so that a hacker can get into the computer?
o: Trojan horse
Worm
Key logger
Spyware
q.why: A Trojan horse, installed by the user because it looks useful, may delete files or open a back door for a hacker.

q.q: When can an employer legally use key-logging software on its work computers?
o: When it has told staff that the software is being used
At any time, because the employer owns the computers
Only when the anti-virus software has been switched off
Only on computers that are not connected to the network
q.why: Some employers use key-logging software legally on work computers, but they must tell staff.

q.q: How does a worm differ from a virus?
o: A worm needs a host file and only spreads when that file is run
A worm needs no host file and spreads by itself across a network
A worm is disguised as useful software so the user installs it
A worm secretly records keystrokes and sends them to a criminal
q.why: A virus needs a host file and spreads when it is run; a worm needs no host and spreads by itself.

q.q: A pupil writes: 'A Trojan horse is a virus that copies itself into games.' What is wrong with this answer?
o: Trojans only hide inside documents, never inside games or programs
Trojans do not copy themselves; they rely on the user installing them
Trojans spread by themselves across networks, not inside games
Trojans only record keystrokes, so they cannot be found in games
q.why: Viruses replicate; Trojans do not. A Trojan is disguised as useful software and the user installs it.

q.q: Which statement compares key loggers and spyware correctly?
o: A key logger watches websites visited; spyware only captures keys that are pressed
A key logger captures keystrokes; spyware watches wider activity such as websites visited
A key logger spreads across networks by itself; spyware needs a host file to run
A key logger opens a back door for hackers; spyware floods a server with requests
q.why: Both work secretly, but a key logger records keys pressed while spyware monitors wider activity: sites visited, items bought, sometimes screenshots.

q.q: Which of these is a way that malware can get onto a computer?
o: Keeping the operating system updated
Opening an infected email attachment
Downloading only from an official app store
Scanning a USB stick before opening its files
q.why: Opening an infected attachment runs the malware. The other three are good habits that help prevent infection.

q.q: Why can out-of-date software let malware onto a computer?
o: Criminals exploit security holes that updates would have closed
Older operating systems are not able to run a firewall at all
Out-of-date software downloads untrusted files automatically
Older software has no way of asking users for a password
q.why: Unpatched software has security holes that criminals exploit; keeping the OS and apps updated closes them.

q.q: How does anti-virus software recognise malware?
o: It compares files with a database of known malware signatures and watches for suspicious behaviour
It checks data entering and leaving the network against the organisation's security rules
It scrambles every file with a key so that malware cannot read any of the data inside it
It copies every file to a separate drive each night so that infected files can be replaced
q.why: Anti-virus scans files and compares them with known signatures, as well as watching for suspicious behaviour. Checking traffic against rules is what a firewall does.

q.q: When anti-virus software quarantines a file, what does it do?
o: Deletes the file permanently from the disk
Sends the file back to the person who sent it
Moves the file somewhere it cannot run
Repairs the file so it can be opened safely
q.why: Quarantining isolates the file where it cannot run. Deleting is a separate option the software may take.

q.q: Why must anti-virus software be updated regularly?
o: So it can filter more traffic coming in from the internet
So it can recognise malware that has been newly created
So that it can make more frequent backups of the files
So that it runs faster on older operating systems
q.why: New malware appears constantly; updates add new signatures to the database. Filtering traffic is a firewall's job.

q.q: Why can even up-to-date anti-virus software fail to stop some malware?
o: It is only able to scan files once a month
Brand-new malware may not yet be in its database
It cannot scan attachments that arrive by email
It only works while the firewall is switched off
q.why: Anti-virus cannot catch everything: brand-new malware may not yet have a signature in its database.

q.q: When does an anti-virus real-time scan take place?
o: Only at a scheduled time once each week
Only when the computer is restarted
Whenever a file is opened or downloaded
Only when the firewall blocks some traffic
q.why: Real-time scans happen whenever a file is opened or downloaded; scheduled full scans happen as well.

q.q: A youth worker in Dungannon finds an unlabelled USB stick in the club's computer room. What is the safest action before opening any files on it?
o: Copy all its files onto the desktop and then open them
Scan it with up-to-date anti-virus software
Open it on the club's main server to identify the owner
Rename the files on it so that they cannot run
q.why: Infected portable storage is a route for malware, so USB sticks should be scanned before files on them are opened.

q.q: Which answer would earn the mark for 'State one way malware can get onto a computer'?
o: Downloading a free game from an untrusted website
From the internet
Through the computer's network
By a hacker getting into the computer
q.why: Examiners want a specific route such as an untrusted download, an email attachment or an infected USB stick, not a vague 'from the internet'.

q.q: A school finds a virus in files already stored on its file server. Which security method is designed to find and remove it?
o: A firewall
A backup
Read-only access
Anti-virus software
q.why: Anti-virus scans and removes malicious files. A firewall filters network traffic and does not clean files.

q.q: An app pretends to be a popular photo-editing tool but secretly contains spyware. Which route for malware is this?
o: Unpatched software
Infected portable storage
An email attachment
A fake app
q.why: Fake apps pretend to be popular tools but contain spyware. Only downloading from trusted sources such as official app stores reduces this risk.

q.q: Which habit best reduces the risk of malware bundled with 'free' films, games or software?
o: Downloading the files onto a USB stick before opening them
Only downloading from trusted sources such as official app stores
Changing the computer's password after every download
Making sure the screen is locked while files are downloading
q.why: Untrusted downloads from unofficial sites often have malware bundled in, so download only from trusted sources.

q.q: Which is the best description of encryption?
o: Filtering the data that enters or leaves a network using a set of rules
Keeping a separate copy of data so that it can be restored after a loss
Checking a user ID and password against a secure database of users
Scrambling data with an algorithm and a key so it is unreadable without the key
q.why: Encryption scrambles data using an algorithm and a key. The other options describe a firewall, a backup and password checking.

q.q: What is readable data called before it is encrypted, and what is the scrambled data called afterwards?
o: Cipher text, then plain text
Source code, then cipher text
Plain text, then source code
Plain text, then cipher text
q.why: Readable plain text is encrypted into cipher text; decryption turns it back into plain text.

q.q: What is decryption?
o: Turning plain text into cipher text using the key
Turning cipher text back into plain text using the key
Removing malware from a file that has been quarantined
Deleting the key so that nobody can read the data
q.why: Decryption reverses encryption at the other end, turning cipher text back into readable plain text with the key.

q.q: A pupil writes: 'Encryption stops hackers stealing data.' Why would this lose the mark?
o: Encryption only protects data stored on a laptop, never on a network
Encryption deletes the data if a hacker tries to intercept it
Encryption only works on data that is protected by a firewall
Encryption does not stop data being stolen; it stops it being understood
q.why: Encryption does not prevent interception or theft. It makes the data meaningless to anyone without the key.

q.q: A laptop holding encrypted customer records is stolen from a car. What is the main benefit of the encryption?
o: The laptop will refuse to switch on for the thief
The data is automatically deleted from the laptop
The thief cannot understand the data without the key
The data is sent back to the company's server
q.why: If an encrypted laptop is stolen, the data is unreadable to anyone who does not have the key.

q.q: Which of these uses encryption to protect data?
o: A Wi-Fi network secured with WPA3
An ordinary website using HTTP
A file sent using basic FTP
A password shown as asterisks
q.why: Encryption is used for Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3), HTTPS websites, messaging apps and encrypted devices. HTTP and basic FTP send data unencrypted; asterisks just hide the password on screen.

q.q: A shift cipher moves each letter 3 places forward in the alphabet. What does CAT become?
o: FDW
DBU
ZXQ
FDX
q.why: C+3 = F, A+3 = D, T+3 = W, giving FDW. DBU uses a shift of 1 and ZXQ shifts backwards.

q.q: A shift cipher moved each letter 2 places forward. The cipher text received is KV. What was the plain text?
o: MX
JU
IS
IT
q.why: To decrypt, move each letter 2 places back: K-2 = I and V-2 = T, giving IT. MX is what you get by shifting forward again.

q.q: In a simple shift cipher, what is the key?
o: The message before it has been scrambled
The scrambled message that is sent
The number of places each letter is moved
The password used to log on to the PC
q.why: The key is the secret needed to encrypt and decrypt; in a shift cipher it is how many places each letter moves.

q.q: How does a network decide whether to let a user log on?
o: It checks the user's files against a database of known malware signatures
It checks the data the user sends against the firewall's set of rules
It checks the user ID and password pair against its secure user database
It checks that the password has been typed in twice in exactly the same way
q.why: Each user has a unique ID and password, and the system checks the pair against its secure user database; if they do not match, access is refused.

q.q: Why are passwords shown as dots or asterisks while they are being typed?
o: So the password is encrypted as it is sent
So the system can measure how strong it is
So a key logger cannot record the keys
So people nearby cannot read them
q.why: The dots stop people nearby reading the password on screen. They do not encrypt it, and a key logger records the keys pressed anyway.

q.q: How do unique user IDs help a network manager?
o: They stop any malware entering the network from outside
They show who logged on, when and from which computer
They make every password on the network much stronger
They let all users share the same set of files safely
q.why: Unique IDs let the network manager log who logged on, when and from which computer.

q.q: Which of these is the strongest password?
o: k9#Vw!2rQz7L
Enniskillen2010
Password123!
enniskillen
q.why: A strong password is long, mixes upper and lower case, digits and symbols and is not a dictionary word or personal detail. The others are based on words or places.

q.q: Why is Liam2010 a weak password even though it contains letters and digits?
o: It does not contain any lower case letters
It is too long to be remembered easily
It contains digits, which make it easier to crack
It is based on personal details that could be guessed
q.why: Passwords based on names or birth years are easy to guess; strong passwords are not dictionary words or personal details.

q.q: After typing her password, a pupil must also enter a code sent to her phone. Why does this improve security?
o: The password is encrypted twice before it is sent
The phone code makes the password itself longer
A stolen password alone is not enough to log on
The phone code replaces the need for a password
q.why: Two-factor authentication adds a second check, so a criminal with only the password cannot get in.

q.q: Why do many systems lock an account after several failed log-on attempts?
o: To force users to change their password every month
To save space in the secure user database
To stop someone repeatedly guessing the password
To stop the server being flooded by a DoS attack
q.why: Locking the account after several failed attempts stops a person trying password after password until one works.

q.q: Pupils can open a homework sheet on the network but cannot make any changes to it. Which level of access do they have?
o: Read and copy
Read and write
Read only
No access
q.why: Viewing without being able to change is read only.

q.q: Pupils can open a template and save their own copy of it in their area, but cannot change the original. Which level of access is this?
o: Read only
Read and write
Read and copy
Full control
q.why: Read and copy lets users view and make their own copy without changing the original.

q.q: Which level of access would a network manager normally have?
o: Full control
Read and write
Read and copy
Read only
q.why: Full control allows changing settings and permissions, which the network manager needs.

q.q: Teachers need to view pupils' marks and also change, add or delete them. Which level of access do they need?
o: Read only
Read and copy
No access
Read and write
q.why: Read and write lets users view and change, add or delete data.

q.q: In a hospital, receptionists can see appointment times but only clinical staff can open medical notes. Which protection method is this?
o: A firewall
Encryption
Levels of access
A backup
q.why: Levels of access give each user only the rights they need, keeping confidential data private.

q.q: Which is a reason for giving each user only the access they need?
o: It means backups no longer need to be made
It limits the damage if one user's login is stolen
It stops malware arriving in email attachments
It makes the network transfer data more quickly
q.why: Giving minimum access keeps confidential data private, stops accidental or deliberate changes and limits the damage if a login is stolen.

q.q: How does a network know which access rights a user has?
o: They are stored in a table linked to each user ID and checked when a file is opened
They are written into each file when it is first saved and cannot be changed
They are checked by the firewall when the user's data leaves the network
They are decided by the anti-virus software each time it scans a file
q.why: Access rights are stored in a table linked to each user ID and checked every time a file is opened.

q.q: What is a backup?
o: A set of rules that filters data entering and leaving a network
A way of scrambling data so it cannot be read without a key
A copy of data kept separately so it can be restored if the original is lost
A record of which users have opened which files and when
q.why: A backup is a separate copy of data that can be restored if the original is lost, corrupted, deleted or stolen.

q.q: A small business keeps its backup drive on a shelf beside its server. What is the main risk?
o: The backup will take much longer to restore if needed
The backup cannot be scheduled to run automatically
Hackers will be able to reach the backup through the firewall
A fire or theft could destroy both the original and the backup
q.why: Backups should be stored away from the original, off site or in the cloud, so one fire or theft does not destroy both.

q.q: Ransomware has scrambled all the files on a company's server. Which protection method is the main defence that lets the company recover its data?
o: A firewall
Read-only access
Strong passwords
Backups
q.why: Backups are the main defence against ransomware because the files can be restored from the separate copy.

q.q: A school wants to stop hackers on the internet getting into its network. Which protection method is designed for this?
o: Anti-virus software
A firewall
A backup
Read and copy access
q.why: A firewall monitors and filters traffic entering or leaving a network and can stop hackers getting in from the internet.

q.q: How does a firewall decide whether data can pass?
o: It compares files with known malware signatures
It asks the user to approve every message
It scrambles the data so it cannot be read
It checks the traffic against a set of rules
q.why: A firewall checks traffic against rules (the organisation's security policy); allowed traffic passes and everything else is blocked.

q.q: Which statement about backups is correct?
o: A backup stops ransomware from being able to infect the server
A backup does not prevent an attack, but lets data be recovered afterwards
A backup filters harmful traffic before it reaches the network
A backup removes the need for anti-virus software on the network
q.why: A backup does not prevent an attack; it lets you recover afterwards. Match the method to the threat.

q.q: Why should network backups be tested regularly?
o: To make sure the data can actually be restored
To stop the backup being stolen from the site
To check the backup is not visible to pupils
To make the backup run more quickly each night
q.why: Backups should be tested regularly so the organisation knows the restore will actually work when needed.

q.q: What is a protocol?
o: A device that connects two different networks together
A program that is installed to connect to the internet
An agreed set of rules for sending and receiving data
A type of cable used to connect devices on a network
q.why: A protocol is a set of rules, not a piece of hardware or a program you install.

q.q: Which area of a protocol's rules lets the receiver know if data has been corrupted so it can ask for it to be resent?
o: Addressing
Format
Speed and timing
Error checking
q.why: Error checking rules say how the receiver knows data is corrupted and asks for it to be resent.

q.q: Which area of a protocol's rules makes sure data reaches the right device?
o: Error checking
Addressing
Format
Speed and timing
q.why: Addressing rules say how the destination is identified so the data reaches the right device.

q.q: Which area of a protocol's rules says where the address goes and where the content starts?
o: Format
Addressing
Error checking
Starting and ending
q.why: The format rules cover how the data is laid out. Addressing is about identifying the destination itself.

q.q: A receiver sends a message to confirm all the data has arrived, and then the connection is closed. Which area of a protocol's rules covers this?
o: Error checking
Starting and ending
Addressing
Speed and timing
q.why: Starting and ending rules cover opening a connection, confirming the data has arrived and closing the connection.

q.q: A phone from one manufacturer, a laptop from another and a smart TV from a third can all exchange data. Why?
o: They all use the same make of router
They all run the same operating system
They all follow the same agreed protocols
They all use the same anti-virus software
q.why: Protocols are agreed standards, so devices from different manufacturers can communicate.

q.q: In TCP/IP, what is the job of TCP?
o: It gives each packet the destination IP address for routing
It requests web pages from a server and returns them
It splits data into packets and checks that they all arrive
It encrypts the data sent between a browser and a server
q.why: TCP splits data into packets and checks they all arrive; IP gives each packet the destination address.

q.q: In TCP/IP, what is the job of IP?
o: It splits the data into packets and checks that every packet has arrived
It transfers files such as a website's pages from a client up to a server
It gives each packet the destination IP address so routers can send it the right way
It checks each packet for malware before it is allowed onto the network
q.why: IP gives each packet the destination IP address so routers can send it along the right path.

q.q: Which statement correctly describes what would happen if there were no agreed protocols?
o: Devices would still communicate, but data would arrive without any encryption
All devices would have to be connected by cable instead of using Wi-Fi
Each company would invent its own rules, so devices could not talk to each other
Data could only be sent between devices that were made in the same country
q.why: Without agreed standards each company would invent its own rules and devices could not exchange data.

q.q: A pupil writes 'A protocol is a set of rules' for a two-mark question. Which addition would earn the second mark?
o: ...which is installed on the computer like any other program
...which is a piece of hardware found inside the router
...that is mainly used to stop hackers getting into a network
...so that devices from different manufacturers can communicate
q.why: The second mark needs a detail about what the rules cover or why they matter, such as letting devices from different manufacturers communicate.

q.q: What does the acronym HTTPS stand for?
o: HyperText Transmission Protocol Secure
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure
HyperText Transfer Program Secure
HyperLink Text Transfer Protocol Secure
q.why: HTTPS is HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure; every word must be spelled correctly when expanding it.

q.q: A web designer needs to upload a new website's files to a web server. Which protocol is designed for this?
o: FTP
HTTP
HTTPS
TCP
q.why: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) uploads and downloads files between computers, such as a website's files to a web server.

q.q: What is the purpose of HTTP?
o: Uploading and downloading files between a client computer and a file server
Splitting data into packets and checking that each packet has arrived
Requesting web pages from a web server and transferring them to a browser
Encrypting the data sent between a browser and a web server using TLS
q.why: HTTP is how the web works: the browser sends a request and the server sends back the page.

q.q: When you click a link, what happens in HTTP?
o: The server sends the page and the browser then sends a request to confirm it
The browser sends a request and the server sends back the page in a response
The browser uploads the page to the server and waits for a status code
The router fetches the page and stores it in the browser's cache
q.why: The browser sends an HTTP request to the web server and the server returns the page in an HTTP response.

q.q: A pupil types a web address for a page that does not exist. Which status code is the server most likely to send back?
o: 404 Not Found
200 OK
301 Moved Permanently
500 Internal Server Error
q.why: If the page cannot be found, the server replies with a status code such as 404 Not Found.

q.q: What technology does HTTPS use to encrypt data?
o: SSL, which replaced the older TLS
FTP, which replaced the older HTTP
TLS, which replaced the older SSL
TCP, which replaced the older IP
q.why: HTTPS encrypts data using TLS, which replaced the older SSL.

q.q: A browser shows a padlock beside a web address. What does this tell the user?
o: The website is owned by an honest company
The connection to the site is encrypted
The website cannot be a phishing site
The website contains no malware at all
q.why: The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest; phishing sites can use HTTPS too.

q.q: Why are secure versions such as SFTP or FTPS used for sensitive files instead of basic FTP?
o: Basic FTP cannot upload large files
Basic FTP sends data unencrypted
Basic FTP does not need a login
Basic FTP only works within a LAN
q.why: Basic FTP sends data unencrypted, so secure versions are used for sensitive files.

q.q: An online shop is building the page where customers enter their card details. Which protocol should the page use?
o: HTTP
FTP
HTTPS
TCP only
q.why: HTTPS encrypts the data, so card numbers are meaningless if intercepted. It should be used whenever personal details are entered.

q.q: Card details are sent from a browser to a website using plain HTTP and are intercepted. What is the result?
o: The card numbers are scrambled and meaningless to them
The data is blocked by the browser before it is sent
The server replies with a 404 Not Found status code
The card numbers can be read by whoever intercepted them
q.why: HTTP sends data as plain text, so intercepted card numbers can be read. With HTTPS they would be scrambled.

q.q: Which is the key difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
o: HTTPS encrypts the data sent between browser and server
HTTPS transfers files while HTTP only transfers web pages
HTTPS uses a web server while HTTP connects directly
HTTPS splits data into packets while HTTP does not
q.why: HTTPS does the same job as HTTP but the data is encrypted; that is the key point to compare.
